oneSentence: The pattern of values, categories and frequencies in a dataset, including what appears often, rarely or not at all.
plainExplanation:
A dataset does not just contain items. It also has a pattern. Some words, numbers or categories appear a lot. Others appear rarely. That overall pattern is the data distribution.

What goes in is a collection of examples: documents, images, records or sensor readings. What happens is that we count, group or measure their features, such as language, length, topic, class label or numeric range. What comes out is a picture of how common different kinds of cases are.

This matters because models fit patterns in the examples they are given. If one type of case dominates the dataset, it has more influence on training, but frequency alone does not determine performance. A balanced dataset is not always the goal, but the distribution should fit the real task.

Data distribution is often confused with sampling and with distribution shift. Sampling is how you select data. Distribution is the pattern in the data you ended up with. Distribution shift is what we call it when that pattern changes between training and real-world use.

everydayAnalogy.title: A tin of assorted buttons
everydayAnalogy.story: Open a sewing tin and you may find many small black buttons, several white ones, one large wooden button and no zips. That pattern is the distribution: which categories are present and how frequently each occurs. If you learned what sewing supplies look like only from this tin, you would become very familiar with black buttons but would be poorly prepared to identify a zip. The tin is not necessarily faulty. It simply may not match what you later encounter.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A book trolley is easy to inspect by eye, but real datasets can have many features at once, such as language, length, source and label. Also, a dataset distribution is often measured with statistics, not just a quick visual impression. Finally, library returns are shaped by human borrowing behaviour, while model data can be shaped by sensors, collection rules, filtering and labelling choices as well.

visual.title: Same task, different data distributions
visual.learningObjective: Show how two datasets can contain the same kinds of items but in different proportions, which changes what a model is likely to learn well.
visual.description: Two side-by-side panels show datasets for the same document-search task. Each panel has 100 document cards split by topic colour: health, education, climate and logistics. Read left to right: first compare the proportions, then see the note below each panel about likely model behaviour.

steps.label: Dataset A
steps.explanation: Most documents are about health, with smaller numbers from other topics.
steps.visualInstruction: Render 100 small cards in a grid. Colour about 70 health, 15 education, 10 climate and 5 logistics. Add a legend and percentages.

steps.label: Dataset B
steps.explanation: The same four topics appear, but the mix is closer to the intended use case.
steps.visualInstruction: Render a second 100-card grid. Colour about 30 health, 25 education, 25 climate and 20 logistics. Keep the same legend and scale.

steps.label: Compare the pattern
steps.explanation: Both datasets include the same topics, but one over-represents health documents.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a bracket or highlight under each panel with a short caption: 'same categories' and 'different proportions'.

steps.label: Likely effect
steps.explanation: A model trained on Dataset A may perform better on health-related searches and less reliably on logistics queries because it saw fewer examples.
steps.visualInstruction: Place one short outcome note under each panel, using arrows from panel to note. No decorative icons.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap a topic in the legend to highlight that topic in both panels and display its count and percentage.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two datasets for the same policy-document search task. Both contain health, education, climate and logistics documents. In Dataset A, health dominates: about 70 out of 100 documents are health, while the other topics are much fewer. In Dataset B, the four topics are more evenly represented: about 30 health, 25 education, 25 climate and 20 logistics. The key message is that the categories can be the same while their proportions differ, and those proportions affect what a model is likely to learn well.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the same two static 100-card grids side by side with percentages, captions and outcome notes. Topic highlighting appears instantly on click or keyboard focus, with no animation.

workedExample.scenario: A programme officer in a regional bureau tests a classifier for routing incoming progress reports before a quarterly portfolio review.
workedExample.input: In the training data, delivery updates appear often, partnership and risk issues appear less often, and evaluation follow-up appears rarely. Some combinations of label, source office and language do not appear at all.
process: The officer counts the records under each label, then compares the distribution across source offices, reporting periods and languages.
They prepare a test set that covers every label and source represented in the intended use, rather than allowing the most frequent label to dominate the test.
The classifier handles the common delivery label consistently but often misses rare labels and combinations absent from its training data.
The officer adds reviewed examples for sparse categories and retests, while also checking whether unclear label definitions or inconsistent tagging contributed to the gap.
workedExample.result: The review shows where the training distribution is dense, sparse or unlike the reports the classifier will receive. It supports targeted data collection and testing, without treating distribution alone as proof of what caused each error.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: An associate expert in a Resident Coordinator's Office is preparing the annual workplan review for front-office clearance by close of business. They check a proposed classifier that assigns paragraphs from implementing partner progress reports to outcomes in the results framework.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The associate expert compares how often each outcome, reporting period, source office and language appears in the model's training data. If some outcomes dominate while others are rare or absent, the classifier may look reliable overall but perform poorly on less represented parts of the workplan.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Progress reports may contain personal, confidential or partner-sensitive information. Such material must not be uploaded to a tool that has not been approved for it, because doing so could breach confidentiality and data protection requirements. Use approved systems, minimise the data and review classifications before they enter the file.

whyItMatters: If you do not look at data distribution, you can make poor decisions about quality, fairness, cost and risk. A model may appear accurate in testing but fail on the cases that matter most in practice because those cases were rare in the data. Distribution also affects how you interpret results: a high overall score can hide weak performance on smaller groups, languages or document types. For programme and technical teams, checking distribution helps you ask better questions: Does this dataset match the real setting? Are important cases missing? Are we measuring success on the right mix of examples?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a dataset is large, its distribution will automatically be suitable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Size and suitability are different. A very large dataset can still over-represent easy, common or cheap-to-collect cases and under-represent rare but important ones. What matters is whether the mix matches the task and the population you care about.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A good overall accuracy score means the distribution problem is solved.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Overall accuracy compresses many cases into one number. If common categories dominate the data, a model can score well overall while performing poorly on less frequent categories. Looking at performance by subgroup or category is often necessary.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The best distribution is always perfectly balanced.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Perfect balance is not automatically correct. If the real-world task is genuinely uneven, forcing equal proportions can make evaluation or training less realistic. The goal is not 'balance' by itself but a distribution that fits the purpose and manages risk.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is the shape of a dataset: what kinds of things are in it, and how often each kind appears.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A data distribution describes how values or features are spread across a dataset. For numeric variables, this can mean ranges, central tendency and frequency across intervals. For categorical variables, it means the relative frequencies of classes or labels. In machine learning, the distribution of training data matters because models fit patterns present in that data. If the joint pattern of inputs and labels is uneven, sparse in some regions, or different from deployment conditions, performance can vary sharply across cases. In practice, teams inspect distributions with counts, proportions, histograms, summary statistics and subgroup analysis. This is related to sampling, because collection choices shape the observed distribution, but it is not the same thing as the sampling process itself.

keyTakeaway: Data distribution is the pattern of what appears often, rarely or not at all. A model usually learns the dense parts best, so overall performance can conceal weak results for sparse categories.

quickCheck.question: Two training datasets contain the same document topics, but one has 80% health documents and the other has 30% health documents. What does this show?
options: They have the same distribution because the topic list is the same.
They may lead to different model behaviour because the topic proportions differ.
Only the larger dataset has a distribution.
Distribution matters only after deployment, not during training.
quickCheck.explanation: Data distribution is about the pattern of frequencies, not just which categories exist. If one topic dominates training data, a model may fit that topic better than others, even when the category list is identical.

issues.problem: The phrase "what appears ... not at all" is unclear. A zero frequency can be identified only against a known or expected set of possible categories. Otherwise, something absent is not observable from the dataset alone.
issues.fix: The pattern of values or categories in a dataset, including how often each observed or expected kind appears.

issues.problem: The claim that a model "usually becomes better" at a type of case merely because that type dominates the dataset overstates causation. Frequency can influence training, but performance also depends on difficulty, labels, features, model design and evaluation.
issues.fix: Replace the third paragraph with: "This matters because models fit patterns in the examples they are given. If one type of case dominates the dataset, it has more influence on training, but frequency alone does not determine performance. A balanced dataset is not always the goal, but the distribution should fit the real task."

issues.problem: The visual says Dataset B is closer to the intended use case and Dataset A over-represents health, but it never states the intended-use distribution. Neither claim can be inferred merely because Dataset B is more even.
issues.fix: For Dataset B, use: "The same four topics appear, but the mix is more even across them." For Compare the pattern, use: "Both datasets include the same topics, but one contains a much larger proportion of health documents."

issues.problem: The arithmetic is correct: 6,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 500 = 10,000; 6,000 / 10,000 = 60%; 500 / 10,000 = 5%; and the test results are 44/50 = 88%, 39/50 = 78%, 36/50 = 72% and 24/50 = 48%. However, those figures show an association, not that the training distribution "favoured" health or caused the logistics gap. Topic difficulty, document quality and other factors could explain the difference.
issues.fix: Replace the final process step with: "The team treats the training distribution as one possible cause of the gap, checks other factors, collects more logistics documents and retests." Replace the result with: "The analysis reveals uneven performance alongside uneven topic counts, guiding further checks and targeted data collection without proving that distribution caused the gap."

issues.problem: Option 1 is the only defensible answer. Option 0 is false because equal category lists do not imply equal frequencies. Option 2 is false because datasets of any size have distributions. Option 3 is false because training data has a distribution that can affect model fitting. However, options 2 and 3 are so plainly false that they do little to test understanding.
issues.fix: Use these options: ["They have the same distribution because the topic list is the same.", "They may lead to different model behaviour because the topic proportions differ.", "Distribution applies to numbers, not topic categories.", "The model will behave the same because every topic appears."]
